newsitem.title: FRANCE: FORECAST - France seen reaching deficit goal in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - France seen reaching deficit goal in 1997.

text.p: France could slip slightly in its plan to reduce the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997, were it not for its overwhelming desire to join Europe's monetary union, economists say.
A Reuter poll of 16 economists released on Thursday showed average expectations of a 1997 deficit of 3.2 percent after 4.3 percent this year.

But given the government's determination to reach the three percent target, and its ability to freeze spending along the way if necessary, economists said it should eventually be able to bring the 1997 figure down to three percent.
Next year is the crucial year for deciding which countries qualify to join a single European currency at the launch of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.
"If you take political will into account, the government will be able to freeze credit lines and cancel them subsequently as it did in 1996," Deutsche Bank economist Patrick Mange said.
"In these conditions three percent will be met," he said.
Based on his expectations of economic growth of 2.1 percent next year, he estimated that the deficit would, without adjustments, reach 3.4 percent of GDP.
Philippe Brossard, economist at ABN-Amro, said he was forecasting a deficit next year of three percent, based on a more optimistic growth forecast of three percent.
"Our growth scenario is stronger than others. If it turns out that way, the government will reach its three percent target," he said.
And if there were to be any overshoot, "the government will always have the possibility of freezing or scrapping spending to reach the target", he said.
France has insisted that Europe should interpret strictly a Maastricht treaty requirement that EMU members must reduce budget deficits to, or below, three percent of GDP.

It has also shown it is willing to use whatever measures necessary to reach that goal, announcing last month it would use pension fund money being transferred from France Telecom to the state to cut France's 1997 deficit to three percent.
The 37.5 billion franc transfer from the telecommunications company radically changed economists' views on France's hopes for meeting Maastricht treaty criteria.
In the last Reuter poll in July, economists forecast on average that the deficit would reach 3.6 percent next year after 4.5 percent this year.

Economists say that France and Germany appear determined to avoid any overshooting of the three percent target themselves as this would make it difficult for them to exclude other countries with even bigger budget deficits.
Germany in particular is determined that EMU should be joined only by countries with strong budget positions to ensure the new euro remains as stable as the mark now is.
